issues.description: The algorithm processes elements right-to-left but does not write the reduced value back into nums. Because earlier iterations read nums[i+1] directly (which remains the original, not the reduced value), comparisons are made against stale values and the computed number of operations (or impossibility) can be incorrect.

The implementation uses a while-loop to repeatedly reduce a number, but mathematically at most one effective reduction is possible (a number n > 1 becomes its smallest prime factor, which is prime and cannot be reduced further). The loop is therefore unnecessary and the logic should be simplified to at most one operation per element; this also clarifies reasoning about impossibility.

greatest_proper_divisor checks divisors up to sqrt(n) for each required number. For worst-case inputs (up to 1e5 elements with values up to 1e6) a precomputed smallest-prime-factor sieve would be substantially faster and avoid repeated sqrt scans.

No test files or unit tests were delivered alongside the implementation. The task expected only solution.py, but automated tests (or at least a few unit cases) would make verification and regression detection easier.

The code correctly detects impossibility when a prime number is larger than the allowed target (since a prime cannot be reduced), but because of the first critical issue (not updating nums), this detection may not be applied to the intended comparisons.
